name: Ivan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at Pennick Lettings, a small independent agency on Station Road in an old mill town. I get in at half eight, clear the voicemails from tenants about mould and broken boilers, then I'm on the phone to landlords trying to get them to fix things. Afternoons are viewings, usually four or five flats above shops, and I do the reference checks at night if I'm behind. I like the tenants, honestly, it's the landlords who wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of the day you'd keep if you could only keep one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The viewings. You meet a young couple who've been turned down six times, and you find them a decent place with a landlord who isn't a crook. My partner Lena works in a care home, so we know what it's like to scrape for a deposit. That's the bit that feels like it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the real problem in lettings isn't technology, it's that there aren't enough homes. A bit of software won't fix a town where forty people apply for one flat. I'd probably post something like that and get ignored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved, but not for long. My pay is low and it's mostly a base with a tiny bonus per let, and Mr Pennick has already said this year has been slow. Hype or no hype, I'm one quiet winter from being let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep my head down. We'd cut the takeaways and I'd stop driving to the far viewings and get the bus. I'd also ask about joining a union, because the office has no one standing up for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the landlords wear you out. Does any of that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the landlords stay the same. One of them, Mr Hale, owns nine flats and won't replace a single window, and that won't change because a computer can write the advert faster. If anything the portals would charge us more for the same listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like for you and Lena right now, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about two weeks of money in the bank once rent goes out. Lena's shifts move around, so some months we're fine and some months I'm checking the balance before I buy petrol. Nothing changing just means nothing gets better either.

say: I'd say the **housing shortage** is the real problem in lettings, not technology.
I'd point out that **software** won't fix forty people chasing one flat.
think: I'm privately **relieved**, but my job was already shaky before AI came up.
My **base pay** is low and a slow winter could get me **let go**.
do: Cut **takeaways** and take the **bus** to far viewings to save petrol.
Ask about joining a **union**, since nobody at the agency speaks up for staff.
feel: He feels **tired** and worn down by money, more than by technology.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared of the rent.
fieldNote: Ivan's worry is **rent and thin savings**, and AI barely registers in this world.
He blames **landlords and portals** far more than technology for what's wrong with his job.
Even with nothing changing, **two weeks** of savings keeps him anxious.

steps.text: Keep doing viewings and reference checks at Pennick Lettings as normal
Drop takeaways and take the bus to far viewings
Ask a tenants' or workers' union about joining this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how they squeeze people like me. The bosses get software that writes listings and books viewings, and nobody asks what happens to the staff. I'd be loud about it, online and in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, half of what I do is phones, emails and booking, and that's exactly what you've listed. If a chatbot answers the tenants and books the viewings, my boss Mr Pennick needs one negotiator, not two. I'm not sure it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a union straight away and try to get Carla, who does the other half of the lettings, to join too. We'd cut back hard: no holiday, Lena's car goes and we share mine. I'd check what help we could get with rent if my hours got cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for a meeting you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Pennick would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla, honestly. She's been there longer but she's slower on the phones, and if the phones go to a machine, Mr Pennick will look at the numbers and pick whoever's cheaper. Either way one of us goes, and in this town there are maybe three other agencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would that hold in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold out as long as I could. I don't trust it, and I don't want to train the thing that replaces me. But if Mr Pennick made it part of the job, I'd use it because I can't afford not to.

say: I'd say this is how **bosses** squeeze staff while nobody asks about the workers.
I'd speak up **online** and in the **pub** about software replacing people in lettings.
think: Half my day is **phones, emails and booking**, which is exactly what AI would take.
Pennick would need **one negotiator** instead of two, and it might not be me.
do: Join a **union** and get Carla, the other lettings negotiator, to join too.
Sell Lena's **car**, skip holidays, and check for **rent help** if hours are cut.
feel: He feels **sick** with dread, like waiting for a meeting he knows is coming.
S1.quote: If a chatbot answers the tenants and books the viewings, my boss Mr Pennick needs one negotiator, not two. I'm not sure it's me.
fieldNote: He sees exactly which **parts of his day** AI would swallow and names them himself.
He refuses to **train his replacement**, yet admits he'd give in if his boss insisted.
With only **three other agencies** in town, losing this job means leaving the trade.

steps.text: Join a union and bring Carla from the lettings desk along
Sell Lena's car and share one car between them
Check what rent support they could claim if his hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. I'd be saying the government has to step in, tax the firms using it and pay people while this settles. Otherwise it's just a handful of companies owning everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in this job inside a year. Lettings is listings, references, booking and answering questions, and a machine that can do any thinking work does all that. The viewings might hang on a bit, but landlords would just send a code for a lockbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really have a plan, that's the truth. We'd probably have to move in with Lena's mum, who has a spare room two towns over. I'd sign on for whatever help there is and go to every meeting about it I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest gets tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena the night you realised this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're going to be all right because she still has the care home. Then I'd go and sit in the car for a bit. Her job is hands-on, so she's got those three years, but I'm sitting behind a screen half the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI comes first and robots three years later. Does that gap matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters for Lena, not much for me. The bit of my job that's hands-on is showing a flat and handing over keys, and you don't need a robot for that, just a key safe. So the three years buys me nothing.

say: I'd demand the **government** taxes firms using AI and pays people through it.
I'd warn that a few **companies** would end up owning everything.
think: I'd be **finished** in lettings within a year, because it's mostly thinking work.
Landlords would swap viewings for a **lockbox code**, so even that part goes.
do: Move in with Lena's **mum**, who has a spare room two towns over.
Sign on for any **government help** and attend every meeting on it.
feel: He feels **panicky**, with a tight chest and no plan.
S2.quote: The bit of my job that's hands-on is showing a flat and handing over keys, and you don't need a robot for that, just a key safe.
fieldNote: He openly says he has **no plan**, which is what tips him into panic.
He sees **Lena's care work** as the household's lifeline because it is hands-on.
The robot gap gives him **nothing**, since a key safe already replaces his viewings.

steps.text: Move in with Lena's mum to stop paying rent
Sign on for any income support available
Go to local meetings calling for taxes on firms using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but I'd add that five years is enough time to do something, if anyone bothers. Unions and councils should be planning now. I'd probably say it at a union meeting rather than online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still means the end of lettings for me, just later. The difference is I'd be thirty-two, not twenty-eight, and maybe I could have something else lined up. I'd still be behind people who started early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an electrician's course at the college at night, because hands-on work gets three more years. I'd put a little away every month, even forty or fifty, which sounds like nothing but it's more than we save now. And I'd stay in the union and push for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen. There's something to grab hold of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years to see it coming, what would you start on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the college. My uncle did wiring for years, and he always said I should've gone that way. It's a few evenings a week and I could keep doing lettings in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new things. How would a trade course sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I hate starting from the bottom, and I'd be the oldest one in the class. But with five years' warning I'd rather be the old one in the class than the one with nothing at the end.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan if unions and councils start now.
I'd raise it at a **union meeting** rather than online.
think: Lettings still **ends** for me, but I'd be thirty-two with something lined up.
I'd still feel **behind** the people who moved early.
do: Enrol in an evening **electrician's course** at the local college.
Save **fifty** a month and push for retraining **money**.
feel: He's **scared** but less frozen, because there's something to grab hold of.
S3.quote: With five years' warning I'd rather be the old one in the class than the one with nothing at the end.
fieldNote: Five years turns his panic into a **plan**, though he still expects to lose lettings.
He chooses **electrical work** because hands-on jobs get the extra three years.
His uncle's old advice gives the plan a **family root**.

steps.text: Start an evening electrician's course at the town college
Put away forty or fifty a month from his pay
Press the union to fund retraining for agency staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is two elections, so I'd be telling people to vote for whoever has a real plan for workers. I'd still be the annoying one at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I actually used the time, and I know I might not. I'm the kind of person who waits until the boiler breaks before calling anyone. That's what worries me about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrician's course properly, full apprenticeship, while Lena keeps the care home job. I'd save something every month so we're not starting from nothing. And I'd keep doing lettings until the qualification is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a voice saying I'll waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time at your age. Does it change who you'd be by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. Maybe Lena and I would have kids by then, and I'd want them to grow up with a dad who has a trade, not one sitting in an empty agency. That's actually a nice picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not do, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't move to the city chasing some tech job. I've seen friends do that and come back broke. I'd rather stay here and wire people's houses.

say: I'd tell people **ten years** means nobody has an excuse not to plan.
I'd urge friends to **vote** for whoever has a real plan for workers.
think: I'd be **fine** if I used the time, but I tend to wait for things to break.
My own **habit of waiting** worries me more than the AI does.
do: Complete a full **electrician apprenticeship** while still doing lettings in the day.
Save **something every month** so the household isn't starting from nothing.
feel: He feels **calmer**, with a nagging fear he'll **waste** the decade.
S4.quote: I'm the kind of person who waits until the boiler breaks before calling anyone. That's what worries me about myself.
fieldNote: He names his own **avoidance** as the main risk in a slow scenario.
He refuses to **move to the city**, tying his future to his home town.
The decade lets him picture **kids and a trade**, a rare hopeful note.

steps.text: Finish a full electrician apprenticeship over the coming years
Save a set amount each month in a separate account
Vote and campaign for parties with plans for displaced workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time and no money to make a plan. What would help is the government paying people a wage while they retrain, and rules that stop landlords and big firms grabbing all the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. If agents disappear, nobody's left to chase the bad landlords, and the people renting the worst flats will be on their own.

headlineQuote: If agents disappear, nobody's left to chase the bad landlords, and the people renting the worst flats will be on their own.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** lettings negotiator at a small agency in an old mill town.
He lives with his partner Lena, a **care worker**, on about **two weeks** of savings.
He blames **landlords and portals**, plus big firms, and backs unions and government help.
He never uses **AI**, and his mood climbs from anxious to panicked as AGI comes faster.
Given time, he'd retrain as an **electrician**, though he fears he'll put it off.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because there would be no time or money to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid wage while retraining** would help, plus rules that stop big firms keeping the gains.
